Group theory

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Algebra
OurBigBook.com Words: 48k Articles: 755
A group records reversible operations that can be combined consistently. Group theory studies their subgroups, group homomorphisms, group actions, and quotient groups. A symmetry group makes the abstraction visible: transformations may change individual points while preserving a specified object or its structure. An orbit of a group action records which positions can be exchanged, while a stabilizer subgroup records which operations leave a selected feature fixed.

Transfer (group theory, VG,H​:G⟶H/H′)

Words: 221 Articles: 2
Group theory OurBigBook.com
For a subgroup H of finite index, choose representatives t of right cosets Ht. Write tg=h(t,g)tg​ with h(t,g)∈H. The transfer is VG,H​(g)=∏t​h(t,g)(modH′). Replacing t by at​t multiplies each factor by at​ on the left and atg​−1​ on the right; these cancel in the abelianization because t↦tg​ is a permutation. The identity h(t,g1​g2​)=h(t,g1​)h(tg1​​,g2​) proves the group homomorphism property after multiplying all factors.

Burnside transfer theorem (P⊆Z(NG​(P))⟹G has a normal p-complement)

Words: 157 Articles: 1
Transfer (group theory) OurBigBook.com
The hypothesis makes P abelian and makes any two conjugate elements of P equal. For the latter assertion, Sylow conjugacy inside the centralizer of the target element adjusts a conjugating element into NG​(P), where it centralizes P. Evaluating group transfer to P on an element u∈P, each coset cycle contributes a conjugate of u raised to the cycle length, hence that same power of u. The restriction is consequently u↦u[G:P], an automorphism of the abelian p-group. Transfer is surjective, and its kernel is the required normal p-complement.

Cyclic Sylow subgroup at the least prime gives a normal complement

Words: 65
Burnside transfer theorem OurBigBook.com
Let p be the smallest prime dividing the order of a finite group, and suppose its Sylow subgroup P is cyclic of order pa. Conjugation embeds NG​(P)/CG​(P) into Aut(P), of order pa−1(p−1). Since P⊆CG​(P), this quotient has order prime to p. Its remaining possible prime divisors are smaller than p and cannot divide ∣G∣. Thus NG​(P)=CG​(P), and the Burnside transfer theorem gives a normal p-complement.

Prüfer rank (rkP​(G)=supH≤G, H finitely generated​d(H))

Words: 141 Articles: 1
Group theory OurBigBook.com
The Prüfer rank bounds the number of generators of a group needed for each finitely generated subgroup, without requiring the ambient group to be finitely generated. The additive group Q has Prüfer rank one: any finitely generated subgroup has a common denominator and is cyclic, but no finite collection generates all rational numbers. Prüfer rank cannot increase under taking subgroups or quotients; for quotients, lift a finite generating set and apply the rank bound to the subgroup generated by its lifts.

Prüfer rank bound for extensions (rkP​(G)≤rkP​(N)+rkP​(G/N))

Words: 64
Prüfer rank OurBigBook.com
For a normal subgroup N with Prüfer rank r and quotient of rank s, let H=⟨h1​,…,hk​⟩≤G. Choose at most s elements xj​∈H generating the image of H. Write hi​=wi​(x1​,…,xs​)ni​ with ni​∈N∩H. The finitely generated subgroup ⟨n1​,…,nk​⟩ needs at most r generators, so H needs at most r+s. The full intersection H∩N need not be finitely generated.

Maximal condition on subgroups (max)

Words: 85
Group theory OurBigBook.com
A group has the maximal condition on subgroups when every ascending sequence of subgroups eventually stabilizes. Equivalently, every subgroup is a finitely generated group. If a subgroup were not finitely generated, repeatedly adjoining an element outside the previously generated subgroup would give a strictly ascending sequence. Conversely, generators of the union of an ascending sequence all lie in one term, making that term the whole union. This condition is preserved by group extensions because each subgroup is an extension of its intersection with the kernel by its image in the quotient.

First isomorphism theorem (G/kerφ≅imφ)

Words: 126
Group theory OurBigBook.com
For a group homomorphism φ:G→H, the group isomorphism gkerφ↦φ(g) gives
G/kerφ≅imφ.
(1)
The group kernel records which inputs become indistinguishable, and the image records which outputs actually occur. The first isomorphism theorem says that identifying precisely those indistinguishable inputs gives a group isomorphic to the image. It is one of the general isomorphism theorems. [ref].
For example, reduction modulo three gives a surjective group homomorphism from the additive cyclic group Z/6Z to Z/3Z. Its group kernel is {0,3}. The three cosets {0,3}, {1,4}, and {2,5} become the three outputs zero, one, and two, respectively. Thus
(Z/6Z)/{0,3}≅Z/3Z.
(2)
The quotient group diagram shows both the identification and the resulting operation. More generally, fibres of a group homomorphism are cosets of its kernel explains why this map is well-defined and injective; it is surjective onto the image by definition.

Direct product of groups

Words: 978 Articles: 6
Group theory OurBigBook.com
A direct product combines two groups into one while keeping their operations in separate coordinates. Its underlying set is the Cartesian product G×H, and its group operation is
(g1​,h1​)(g2​,h2​)=(g1​g2​,h1​h2​).
(3)
The identity element is (eG​,eH​), and the inverse element of (g,h) is (g−1,h−1). Associativity follows coordinate by coordinate. For finite groups, the multiplication principle gives ∣G×H∣=∣G∣∣H∣.
For example, write the cyclic group Cm​ as the additive group of residue classes modulo m. In C2​×C3​,
(1,2)+(1,2)=(0,1),
(4)
since each coordinate reduces with its own integer modulus. A pair can track two cyclic counters that advance independently. Updating the first coordinate does not alter the second, and vice versa.
This independence has an algebraic form. The embedded factor elements always commute:
(g,eH​)(eG​,h)=(g,h)=(eG​,h)(g,eH​).
(5)
The coordinate maps (g,h)↦g and (g,h)↦h are group homomorphisms, so one can analyze either component separately. This does not make the full product an abelian group when one of its factors is nonabelian: two arbitrary pairs need not commute.
The construction is useful in both directions. It builds a larger group from familiar pieces, while the internal direct product theorem recognizes when an existing group can be separated into such pieces. A cyclic group can sometimes be split this way; whether two finite cyclic factors combine into one cyclic group is decided by the cyclicity of a product of two finite cyclic groups. Definitions and the basic recognition theorems are developed in Thomas Judson, Abstract Algebra: Theory and Applications, §9.2, Direct Products.

Direct product of cyclic groups of orders four and two (C4​×C2​=⟨c,a∣c4=a2=e, ca=ac⟩)

Words: 138 Articles: 1
Direct product of groups OurBigBook.com
This abelian group has eight elements cras, with r taken modulo four and s modulo two. Its group operation adds these exponent pairs separately. The elements of order two are c2,a,c2a, and the other four nonidentity elements c,c3,ca,c3a have order four. It is a direct product of groups rather than a cyclic group, since no element has order eight.

Subgroups of C4 times C2 (#{H:H≤C4​×C2​}=8)

Words: 86
Direct product of cyclic groups of orders four and two OurBigBook.com
With the generators c,a of the direct product of cyclic groups of orders four and two, the subgroups are the trivial group, the whole group, the three order-two groups ⟨c2⟩, ⟨a⟩, ⟨c2a⟩, and the three order-four groups ⟨c⟩, ⟨ca⟩, ⟨c2,a⟩. These are exhaustive by Lagrange's theorem: a proper nontrivial subgroup has order two or four; an order-four subgroup either contains an element of order four and is one of the two cyclic examples, or is precisely the four-element set killed by squaring. The latter is a Klein four-group.

Cyclicity of a product of two finite cyclic groups (Cm​×Cn​ cyclic ⟺ gcd(m,n)=1)

Words: 183
Direct product of groups OurBigBook.com
For positive integers m,n, two finite cyclic groups combine into one cyclic group precisely when their group orders are coprime:
Cm​×Cn​≅Cmn​⟺gcd(m,n)=1.
(6)
The reason is that both cyclic counters must return to their identity elements simultaneously. If a,b are generators of a group for the two factors, the order of a direct-product element gives ord(a,b)=lcm(m,n). The pair generates all mn elements exactly when this least common multiple is mn.
For C2​×C3​, repeated addition of (1,1) visits
(0,0),(1,1),(0,2),(1,0),(0,1),(1,2),(0,0).
(7)
All six pairs appear before the return, so (1,1) is a generator. In contrast, in C2​×C2​ the same step gives only (0,0),(1,1),(0,0). Every nonidentity element has order of a group element two, so none can generate all four pairs. This is the Klein four-group; there is no group isomorphism to C4​ even though both have four elements.
For a brief proof of the converse, each component order of a group element divides the corresponding factor group order. Every pair's order therefore divides lcm(m,n). If gcd(m,n)>1, this is smaller than mn, so no pair can generate the whole product. The Chinese remainder theorem gives the explicit isomorphism in the coprime case: tmodmn↦(tmodm,tmodn).

Order of a direct-product element (ord(g,h)=lcm(ordg,ordh))

Words: 126
Direct product of groups OurBigBook.com
If the order of a group element is m for g and n for h, with both finite, then
(g,h)k=(gk,hk)=(eG​,eH​)
(8)
exactly when both m and n divide k. The smallest positive such k is their least common multiple, giving
ord(g,h)=lcm(m,n).
(9)
This concerns the orders of the selected elements, which need not equal the orders of their entire groups. If either component has infinite order of a group element, no positive power can return the pair to the identity element, so the pair also has infinite order.
For example, in C4​×C6​, the additive element (2,3) has component orders 2,2, hence pair order 2. The element (1,1) instead has order lcm(4,6)=12. The product has 24 elements, so even this latter element does not generate it. This distinguishes group order from order of a group element while exposing the simultaneous-return interpretation.

Restricted direct sum of groups (⨁i​Gi​)

Words: 60
Direct product of groups OurBigBook.com
The restricted direct sum of a family of groups Gi​ is the subgroup of their direct product of groups consisting of tuples with only finitely many nonidentity coordinates. Multiplication is coordinatewise. If every factor is a finite group, each subgroup that is a finitely generated group lies in a finite subproduct, so the restricted direct sum is a locally finite group. This gives concrete infinite torsion groups without a uniform bound on element orders.

Internal direct product theorem

Words: 259
Direct product of groups OurBigBook.com
An internal direct product finds independent coordinates already present inside a group. Let H,K be normal subgroups of G with
H∩K={e},HK=G.
(10)
Then the multiplication map
Φ:H×K⟶G,Φ(h,k)=hk
(11)
is a group isomorphism. Thus every element of G has a unique factorization into one element of each subgroup. Conversely, the embedded factors G×{eH​} and {eG​}×H inside an external direct product of groups satisfy these conditions.
For a concrete example, take the additive cyclic group C6​=Z/6Z and its subgroups H={0,3} and K={0,2,4}. They are normal subgroups because C6​ is an abelian group. Their intersection is {0}, and the sums h+k give every residue class exactly once. For instance, 1=3+4mod6. The table makes the unique decomposition visible.
The proof explains each hypothesis. Normality puts the group commutator [h,k]=h−1k−1hk in both H and K, so it is the identity element. Therefore the factors commute, and Φ preserves the group operation. The condition HK=G makes it surjective. If hk=e, then h=k−1 belongs to the intersection, forcing both to be the identity element; thus its group kernel is trivial and it is injective.
Normality cannot simply be omitted. In the symmetric group S3​, take H=⟨(123)⟩ and K=⟨(12)⟩. Their intersection is trivial and HK=S3​, but K is not a normal subgroup. With permutations composed right to left, (123)(12)=(13) while (12)(123)=(23), so the factors do not commute. The setwise decomposition is unique, but its multiplication map is not a group homomorphism from H×K. An independent-coordinate interpretation requires the group operations to agree, not merely a bijection of the underlying sets.

Metacyclic group

Words: 22
Group theory OurBigBook.com
A group is metacyclic when it has a cyclic normal subgroup whose quotient is cyclic. Every dihedral group is metacyclic through its rotation subgroup.

Commutator subgroup (G′=[G,G])

Words: 1k Articles: 9
Group theory OurBigBook.com
The commutator subgroup of a group G is the subgroup generated by all its group commutators:
G′=[G,G]=⟨x−1y−1xy:x,y∈G⟩.
(12)
Here and throughout, [x,y]=x−1y−1xy. A group commutator is the identity element precisely when x and y commute. The generated subgroup includes finite products of group commutators and their inverse elements; an element of G′ need not itself be a single group commutator. Thus G′={e} precisely when G is an abelian group.
The useful idea is to record exactly what must disappear to make multiplication commutative. The identity xy=yx[x,y] shows how a group commutator corrects a change in multiplication order. Setting every such correction equal to e produces the abelianization G/G′, while preserving every piece of information that a group homomorphism to an abelian group can detect. This connects a local comparison of two operations to a canonical quotient group of the whole group.
The commutator subgroup is a characteristic subgroup, hence a normal subgroup: a group automorphism α sends [x,y] to [α(x),α(y)]. For any normal subgroup N,
G/N is abelian⟺G′⊆N.
(13)
Indeed, the group commutator of xN and yN is [x,y]N. This makes G′ the smallest normal subgroup whose quotient group is an abelian group. See Conrad, Subgroup series I, section 4: commutators and abelian quotients.

Commutator subgroup of the symmetric group on three letters (S3′​=A3​)

Words: 163
Commutator subgroup OurBigBook.com
For the symmetric group S3​, take the transpositions x=(12) and y=(23). Products of permutations apply the rightmost factor first. Then
xy=(123),yx=(132),[x,y]=(12)(23)(12)(23)=(132).
(14)
The last permutation sends 1↦3, 3↦2, and 2↦1: two swaps fail to commute by an entire three-cycle.
Every group commutator has sign of a permutation +1, so S3′​⊆A3​, the alternating group of even permutations. Conversely, the displayed group commutator generates A3​={e,(123),(132)}. Therefore S3′​=A3​. The two cosets are the even permutations and the odd permutations, and their multiplication is just multiplication of signs:
S3ab​=S3​/A3​≅{+1,−1}≅C2​.
(15)
This is the first isomorphism theorem applied to the sign of a permutation. Once commutativity is forced, all three transpositions become indistinguishable, and both three-cycles become the identity element. The surviving information is exactly whether the permutation is even or odd. Compare the very different center of a group Z(S3​)={e}.

where G′ is the commutator subgroup. Its elements are cosets, and its operation is (gG′)(hG′)=ghG′. The result is an abelian group: the two products gh and hg differ by a group commutator, which disappears in the quotient group.
For the symmetric group S3​, the sign of a permutation realizes S3ab​≅C2​, as shown in commutator subgroup of the symmetric group on three letters. For the dihedral group of a square, abelianization of the square symmetry group gives C2​×C2​: two independent yes-or-no pieces of information survive. An abelian group already has G′={e}, so its abelianization is isomorphic to itself. At the other extreme, a perfect group has trivial abelianization.
Calling this the largest abelian quotient means that every group homomorphism into any abelian group factors uniquely through q. It does not require G to be finite, or compare the sizes of unrelated abelian groups. The universal property of abelianization makes this precise. It lets us solve all such mapping problems in one simpler group: any invariant that respects multiplication and takes values in an abelian group sees only Gab.

Group theory OurBigBook.com
The center of a group consists of the elements that commute with every element of that group:
Z(G)={z∈G:zg=gz for every g∈G}=⋂g∈G​CG​(g),
(23)
where CG​(g) is the centralizer of g. These are operations whose position in any product can be changed freely. The center is an abelian group and a characteristic subgroup, hence a normal subgroup. A group is an abelian group precisely when Z(G)=G.
For the symmetric group S3​, the conjugacy classes are
{e},{(12),(13),(23)},{(123),(132)}.
(24)
An element belongs to the center precisely when its conjugacy class has one element, so Z(S3​)={e}. Yet commutator subgroup of the symmetric group on three letters gives S3′​=A3​, with three elements. Thus belonging to the commutator subgroup does not mean commuting with everything. The alternating group A3​ is an abelian group as a subgroup, but its nonidentity elements do not commute with the transpositions in the surrounding S3​.
For the dihedral group D8​ of group order eight in abelianization of the square symmetry group, the center is {e,r2}. A rotation ri commutes with s precisely when ri=r−i, which requires i even. No reflection ris commutes with r, since (ris)r=ri−1s whereas r(ris)=ri+1s. Consequently
Z(D8​)={e,r2}=D8′​.
(25)
The half-turn can be performed before or after any square symmetry with the same result. Its appearance both here and in the commutator subgroup is a feature of this example, rather than a general equality. See Conrad, Dihedral groups I, theorem 3.4 and example 3.5.
The center and the commutator subgroup answer different useful questions: which operations already commute with everything, and which operations must disappear for the entire group to commute. In an abelian group these answers are Z(G)=G and G′={e}. Another way to use the center is through conjugation: the group homomorphism g↦(h↦ghg−1) has group kernel Z(G), so the first isomorphism theorem gives G/Z(G)≅Inn(G), the inner automorphism group. The quotient group by the center thus records the distinct conjugation operations; it need not be an abelian quotient.
A nontrivial finite p-group always has a nontrivial center. In the class equation, each noncentral conjugacy class has size divisible by p, so ∣Z(G)∣≡∣G∣≡0(modp). The identity element ensures Z(G) is nonempty, hence it has at least p elements. See McKernan, MIT 18.703, lemmas 23.6–23.7 and definition-lemma 23.10.

Coset (gH, Hg)

Words: 890 Articles: 8
Group theory OurBigBook.com
For a subgroup H≤G of a group G, a left coset is gH={gh:h∈H}; a right coset is Hg={hg:h∈H}. The name refers to the side on which the representative g multiplies H. Think of a coset as a translated copy of a subgroup: it remembers the relative differences allowed by H, while moving the whole collection to another location in the group.
Two left cosets of the same subgroup are either equal or disjoint. Thus distinct left cosets form a partition of a set covering G; the same statement holds separately for right cosets. The useful membership test is
aH=bH⟺b−1a∈H.
(29)
This also defines an equivalence relation: changing a representative by right multiplication with a member of H leaves its left coset unchanged. These facts hold even for infinite groups. See MIT's coset notes, definitions 3.6 and 3.9.
For an explicit additive example, take the cyclic group G=Z/6Z, with modular arithmetic, and the subgroup H={0,3}. Adding each representative to both members gives exactly
0+H={0,3},1+H={1,4},2+H={2,5}.
(30)
Representatives 3,4,5 repeat these three cosets, respectively. For example, 4+H={4,1}=1+H, since 4−1=3∈H. Every residue appears once in the displayed partition of a set. Each coset has two members, so the group order of H is 2 and its index of a subgroup is 3. Left and right cosets coincide here because G is an abelian group.
A coset need not be a subgroup. In this example, {1,4} lacks the identity element 0, and 1+1=2 leaves it. In fact, the only left or right coset of H that is a subgroup is H itself: a subgroup must contain the identity element, and the coset containing that element is H. Equal sizes come instead from the bijection h↦gh, whose inverse is x↦g−1x; for right cosets, use h↦hg and x↦xg−1.
The nonabelian group S3​, the symmetric group on three letters, separates the two sides. Use function composition with the rightmost permutation applied first, and let H={e,(12)}. Then (13)(12)=(123) but (12)(13)=(132), giving the differing pair
(13)H={(13),(123)},H(13)={(13),(132)}.
(31)
The complete partition of a set into left cosets consists of H, {(13),(123)} and {(23),(132)}; the complete partition of a set into right cosets consists of H, {(13),(132)} and {(23),(123)}. Each lists all six permutations exactly once. Both have three parts of size two, although their parts differ.
Left cosets support a group action by a⋅(gH)=(ag)H for every subgroup, as in the coset action. Multiplication of representatives defines a quotient group operation (aH)(bH)=(ab)H precisely when H is a normal subgroup. Otherwise the answer can depend on the representatives: in this S3​ example, e and (12) represent the same coset H, yet e(13)H=(13)H and (12)(13)H=(23)H differ. In the additive example, H is a normal subgroup, making (1+H)+(2+H)=3+H=H valid. See MIT's quotient-group notes, theorem 9.1.

Lagrange's theorem (∣G∣=[G:H]∣H∣)

Words: 444 Articles: 1
Group theory OurBigBook.com
For a finite group G and a subgroup H, the group order of H divides the group order of G:
∣G∣=[G:H]∣H∣.
(36)
Here [G:H] is the index of a subgroup, the number of distinct left cosets. It is also the number of distinct right cosets: inversion gives a bijection gH↦Hg−1 between the two collections. No normal subgroup assumption is needed for Lagrange's theorem. The normal subgroup condition matters when constructing a quotient group, rather than when counting a partition of a set.
The beauty of Lagrange's theorem is that an arithmetic restriction follows from a structural picture. A group can be tiled by equal-sized cosets of any subgroup. To see the count, choose one representative from each left coset. Every group element has exactly one expression gi​h for these chosen representatives and h∈H: different rows do not overlap, and multiplication by gi​ is a bijection from H to its row. Counting rows times row size gives the formula. See MIT's symmetries notes, section 2.
The additive cyclic group Z/6Z above gives 6=3×2 from H={0,3}. Another subgroup, K={0,2,4}, has cosets K and 1+K={1,3,5}, giving 6=2×3. In S3​, the subgroup {e,(12)} also gives 6=3×2, despite its distinct left and right coset partitions. Thus equal row sizes persist in a nonabelian group. A proposed subgroup of size four in either group is impossible: four does not divide six. This filters possible subgroups before any search for group generators.
Apply Lagrange's theorem to the cyclic subgroup generated by a group element g. Its size is the order of a group element, so ord(g)∣∣G∣ and g∣G∣=e. In the additive example, 2 has order of a group element 3, since 2+2+2=0 modulo six; the corresponding multiplicative statement becomes 6⋅2=0. A group of prime group order is consequently a cyclic group: any nonidentity group element generates a subgroup whose size is greater than one and divides that prime, forcing it to be the whole group. See MIT's cyclic-group notes. The same counting idea underlies the orbit-stabilizer theorem: the orbit of a group action is parametrized by cosets of its stabilizer subgroup.
Historically, Lagrange's theorem grew from investigations of permutations of roots of a polynomial; see St Andrews' account of Lagrange's early work. The modern statement about arbitrary finite groups should not be read back into the early work. Carmichael's 1921 review explicitly cautioned against attributing the full result to Lagrange; see Carmichael's historical note, reproduced by St Andrews. Finally, Lagrange's theorem supplies a necessary size condition; the failure of the converse to Lagrange's theorem below explains its limit.

Divisibility of a proposed subgroup order is necessary by Lagrange's theorem but is not sufficient in arbitrary finite groups. The alternating group A4​ has order 12 and no subgroup of order 6. Such a subgroup would have index two, hence be a normal subgroup. The quotient would have order two, so every element of order three would map to its identity. But A4​ has eight distinct three-cycles, which together with the identity cannot fit in a subgroup of order six. This obstruction contrasts with cyclic groups, which have a subgroup of every divisor order.

Cayley's theorem

Words: 947 Articles: 1
Group embedding OurBigBook.com
Every group G is isomorphic to a subgroup of the symmetric group on its underlying set. The construction uses the left regular action: each group element g becomes a permutation of all the group elements, given by
Lg​:G⟶G,Lg​(x)=gx,λ:G↪Sym(G),g⟼Lg​.
(37)
For a finite group of group order n, labeling these elements by 1,…,n gives a group embedding into Sn​. The same construction works for an infinite group, with the symmetric group of all bijections of its underlying set.[ref]
The beauty is that the multiplication rule itself supplies a concrete model. Whatever the group elements originally represent, each one rearranges the entire group by multiplication. A product becomes function composition, and no distinctions between group elements are lost. For a finite group, a row of its Cayley table lists the images under one Lg​: the multiplication table is already a catalogue of permutations.
Throughout this construction, products of permutations act rightmost first:
(στ)(x)=(σ∘τ)(x)=σ(τ(x)),Lg​Lh​=Lgh​.
(38)
Thus Lg​Lh​ first multiplies by h, then by g. This is a left group action, not a license to reverse the multiplication order in a nonabelian group. Ordinary right multiplication Rg​(x)=xg instead satisfies Rg​Rh​=Rhg​ with this convention; replacing it by x↦xg−1 restores the group homomorphism law.[ref]
For an explicit cyclic group example, take C4​=Z/4Z under addition, using modular arithmetic. Its left regular action consists of Lk​(x)=k+x(mod4). In permutation cycles on the labels 0,1,2,3,
L0​=id,L1​=(0 1 2 3),L2​=(0 2)(1 3),L3​=(0 3 2 1).
(39)
The function composition L1​L1​=L2​ sends 0 to 2, 1 to 3, 2 to 0, and 3 to 1: squaring the four-point permutation cycle produces two disjoint permutation cycles. Also L1​L3​=L0​. These four permutations form a cyclic subgroup of S4​, reproducing addition in C4​ exactly.
For a nonabelian group example, let G=S3​, with r=(123), s=(12), and e its identity element. The six group elements are e,r,r2,s,rs,r2s, where r3=s2=e and sr=r2s. Now the labels being permuted are themselves permutations of three points. Computing the left regular action gives permutations of these six labels:
Lr​=(e r r2)(s rs r2s),Ls​=(e s)(r r2s)(r2 rs).
(40)
For example, Ls​(r)=sr=r2s; putting rs here would accidentally switch to right multiplication. Noncommutativity survives in the model:
(Lr​Ls​)(e)=rs=(13),(Ls​Lr​)(e)=sr=(23).
(41)
These different outputs prove that Lr​Ls​=Ls​Lr​. The group generators r,s become group generators Lr​,Ls​ of a six-element subgroup of S6​.
Why does a group action here produce a group embedding? Any group action on a set X gives a group homomorphism ρ:G→Sym(X); it is a group embedding precisely when it is a faithful group action. The group kernel consists of the group elements fixing every point of X. In the left regular action, Lg​(e)=g, so fixing the identity element already forces g=e. In fact every stabilizer subgroup is trivial, since gx=x forces g=e; this stronger property makes the left regular action a regular group action.[ref]
Compare two group actions of the same cyclic group C4​. Its left regular action on four labels distinguishes all four group elements. On X={0,1}, the rule k⋅x=k+x(mod2) defines a transitive group action, but 0 and 2 both fix both points, while 1 and 3 both exchange them. Its group kernel is {0,2}, so it is not a faithful group action. Its image is a two-element subgroup of S2​, isomorphic to the quotient group C4​/{0,2} rather than to C4​.
The guaranteed number ∣G∣ of labels need not be the smallest possible for a faithful group action. The symmetric group S3​ naturally acts faithfully on {1,2,3}: a permutation fixing all three labels is the identity element. Its left regular action uses six labels instead. Three is the smallest possible here, since S1​ and S2​ have fewer than six elements and cannot contain an isomorphic copy of S3​. Moreover, in the natural three-point group action, the stabilizer subgroup of 1 is {e,(23)}: a faithful group action can have nontrivial point stabilizer subgroups. Cayley's construction supplies a universal model, while a smaller model can reveal particular symmetries.
The proof is short. Each Lg​ is a bijection with inverse Lg−1​. Associativity gives
Lg​(Lh​(x))=g(hx)=(gh)x=Lgh​(x),
(42)
so λ is a group homomorphism. If Lg​=Lh​, evaluating both at the identity element gives g=Lg​(e)=Lh​(e)=h. Hence λ is injective, and its image is the required isomorphic subgroup. No finiteness assumption entered the argument.
The historical connection is unusually close to the notation. The opening paragraph of Arthur Cayley's 1854 paper already treats permutations as one example of operations on a collection of quantities and explicitly performs the rightmost operation first in a product. It also allows noncommutativity while insisting on associativity. The modern left regular action shows how that viewpoint reaches every abstract group, by choosing the group itself as the set to be acted on.[ref]

Group theory OurBigBook.com
For a group G and a normal subgroup N, the quotient group G/N is the set of cosets gN, with operation
(gN)(hN)=(gh)N.
(44)
Its identity element is the coset N, and the inverse element of gN is g−1N. A quotient group treats all elements within one coset as the same input while retaining a consistent operation on the classes. The normal subgroup condition is what makes this operation independent of which representatives are chosen. [ref].
Take the additive group G=Z/6Z and N={0,3}. Since G is an abelian group, N is a normal subgroup. There are three elements in the quotient group:
N={0,3},1+N={1,4},2+N={2,5}.
(45)
Adding two copies of 2+N gives 4+N=1+N; adding 1+N and 2+N gives 3+N=N. Hence the quotient group has the addition table of Z/3Z. It does not select one representative and discard the others: its elements are the entire cosets.
This is useful whenever distinctions within a normal subgroup should be ignored. For example, the sign of a permutation retains only even or odd parity of a permutation in S3​. Its group kernel is the alternating group A3​, and the quotient group S3​/A3​ has two elements. The first isomorphism theorem explains why a group homomorphism's image is a quotient group of its domain.

Group theory OurBigBook.com
A group homomorphism is a map φ:G→H preserving the group operation: φ(gh)=φ(g)φ(h). It also preserves the identity element and inverse elements. In an additive group, the same requirement reads φ(g+h)=φ(g)+φ(h). A group homomorphism preserves a way of combining inputs, even when several inputs have the same output.
Reduction modulo three from Z/6Z to Z/3Z is a group homomorphism: reducing a sum agrees with adding the reduced residues. For example, 2+5=1 modulo six, and both sides reduce to one modulo three; the outputs 2 and 2 also add to one modulo three. This map is surjective but not injective, since zero and three both map to zero.
The sign of a permutation gives another example, from the symmetric group S3​ to the multiplicative group {1,−1}. A product of two odd permutations is even, matching (−1)(−1)=1. Its group kernel is A3​, the alternating group of even permutations. This shows how a group homomorphism can retain a useful feature while forgetting other details.

A nonzero element of a free abelian group is primitive when it is part of an integral basis, equivalently when some homomorphism to Z takes it to one. Its coordinates have greatest common divisor one. This lattice meaning differs from a primitive homology class in the coalgebra sense.

Normal subgroup (N⊴G)

Words: 1k Articles: 24
Group theory OurBigBook.com
A subgroup N≤G is a normal subgroup when gNg−1=N for every g∈G. In other words, conjugation by any group element preserves the subgroup as a set, although it may exchange its individual elements. Equivalently, gN=Ng for every g: the left and right cosets of N agree. Write N⊴G.
Every subgroup of an abelian group is a normal subgroup, because conjugation fixes each element. Normality can also hold in a nonabelian group: in S3​, the three even permutations form the alternating group A3​={e,(123),(132)}, a normal subgroup as the group kernel of the sign of a permutation. Its two cosets separate the even and odd permutations.
In contrast, H={e,(12)} is a subgroup of S3​ but is not a normal subgroup. With function composition of permutations acting rightmost first, choose g=(123). Then
gH={(123),(13)},Hg={(123),(23)},
(57)
which are different cosets. Also g(12)g−1=(23)∈/H, directly contradicting invariance under conjugation. Thus a subgroup alone does not suffice for quotient group multiplication.
The practical value of normality is coset multiplication is well-defined exactly for normal subgroups. Each coset can act as one element of a quotient group, with results independent of representatives. Conversely every normal subgroup is the group kernel of its quotient map of groups, so normality also identifies which distinctions a group homomorphism can consistently forget.

Normal subgroup OurBigBook.com
The p-residual is the smallest normal subgroup with p-group quotient, equivalently the subgroup generated by all elements of order prime to p. It is characteristic and satisfies Op(Op(G))=Op(G): an extension of two finite p-groups is a p-group. A finite group has a normal p-complement exactly when its p-residual has order prime to p.

Normal subgroup OurBigBook.com
A group complement to a normal subgroup N◃G is a subgroup H with G=NH and N∩H=1. Projection identifies H with G/N, and conjugation gives G=N⋊H. This is a subgroup notion, not the set-theoretic complement of N.

Normal subgroups of coprime order commute

Words: 65
Normal subgroup OurBigBook.com
If finite normal subgroups H,K of a group have coprime orders, their intersection is trivial by Lagrange's theorem. For h∈H and k∈K, the commutator hkh−1k−1 belongs to both subgroups: write it as h(kh−1k−1) to use normality of H, and as (hkh−1)k−1 to use normality of K. Hence it is the identity and hk=kh. The product subgroup is therefore isomorphic to the direct product of groups H×K.

Normal subgroup OurBigBook.com
For a finite group with Sylow p-subgroup P, a normal p-complement is a normal subgroup of order ∣G∣/∣P∣. It consists exactly of the elements of order prime to p: every such element has trivial image in the p-group quotient, and every element of the complement has prime-to-p order. Thus a normal p-complement, if it exists, is unique and a characteristic subgroup.

A finite group is p-nilpotent when it has a normal p-complement. This terminology is distinct from having a normal Sylow p-subgroup. A finite group is nilpotent exactly when it is p-nilpotent for every prime dividing its order.

Indeed, the p-prime-degree characters are exactly the linear characters. Their squared-degree sum is ∣G:G′∣, whose p-part is ∣G:G′∣p​; Isaacs' character-degree criterion for p-nilpotency applies.

Invariant p-prime-degree characters of N extend, and each has exactly h extensions of p-prime degree. Conjugation by the p-group G/N then gives s/h≡∣N∣(modp). Normal subgroup OurBigBook.com
A subnormal series is a finite chain of subgroups in which each is a normal subgroup of the next. A member need not be normal in the whole group. Requiring the factors to be cyclic groups defines a polycyclic group; allowing finite factors as well defines a poly-(cyclic or finite) group.

Schreier refinement theorem

Words: 72
Subnormal series OurBigBook.com
Any two finite subnormal series have refinements with the same successive factors up to ordering and group isomorphism. For descending chains Ai​ and Bj​, insert Ai+1​(Ai​∩Bj​) between Ai​ and Ai+1​ and insert Bj+1​(Bj​∩Ai​) in the other chain. The Zassenhaus butterfly lemma identifies the factor indexed by (i,j) in the first refinement with the factor indexed by (j,i) in the second. If both chains are composition series, their simple factors admit no nontrivial refinement, giving the Jordan–Hölder theorem.

A chief series is a strict normal series of a group with no proper normal-series refinement. Its factors are minimal normal subgroups of the appropriate quotient groups. A chief factor of a finite soluble group is elementary abelian, whereas a composition factor of a finite soluble group is cyclic of prime order. A chief factor can therefore have order larger than a prime.

Chief series OurBigBook.com
A chief factor of G is a quotient N/M with M,N normal in G and no G-normal subgroup strictly between them. Equivalently, N/M is a minimal normal subgroup of G/M. Such factors are the successive factors of a chief series, and are direct products of isomorphic simple groups when G is finite.

Minimal normal subgroup

Normal subgroup OurBigBook.com
A minimal normal subgroup is a nontrivial normal subgroup containing no smaller nontrivial normal subgroup of the ambient group. It need not be a minimal nontrivial subgroup. In a finite soluble group, it is elementary abelian: its derived subgroup must be trivial, a characteristic Sylow subgroup selects one prime, and the characteristic subgroup of elements killed by that prime gives exponent p.

Minimal normal subgroups of finite solvable groups are elementary abelian

Words: 45
Minimal normal subgroup OurBigBook.com
A nontrivial minimal normal subgroup N of a finite solvable group is abelian: its commutator subgroup is characteristic, and minimality plus solvability excludes N′=N. A nontrivial Sylow subgroup of this abelian group is characteristic, so minimality makes N a p-group. The characteristic subgroup of pth powers is proper, hence trivial by minimality. Therefore N is an elementary abelian group.

Direct-product structure of a finite minimal normal subgroup (K≅Sr)

Words: 115
Minimal normal subgroup OurBigBook.com
Choose a minimal nontrivial normal subgroup L of K. Its conjugates under the ambient group are minimal normal subgroups of K; distinct ones intersect trivially and commute. Choose a maximal family whose product is direct. Any omitted conjugate either lies in that product or meets it trivially and could be adjoined, so all conjugates lie in it. Their product is ambient-normal and therefore is K. A normal subgroup of one factor is then normal in K, since the other factors commute with it; minimality makes each factor simple. All factors are isomorphic because they are conjugates of L. In the abelian case they are cyclic of one common prime order.

Minimal normal subgroup OurBigBook.com
The socle is generated by all minimal nontrivial normal subgroups. Distinct minimal normal subgroups commute and meet trivially, although in the abelian case not every collection of them is an independent direct-product decomposition. It is a direct product of simple groups. In a faithful primitive permutation group each nontrivial normal subgroup is transitive; its minimal normal subgroups are either elementary abelian and regular, or direct powers of a nonabelian simple group. This is the starting point of the O'Nan–Scott theorem.

The Möbius transformations preserving a three-point set act faithfully on it: one fixing all three is the identity. Möbius group OurBigBook.com
A finite abelian subgroup of the Möbius group is cyclic or isomorphic to C2​×C2​. If it contains an element of order greater than two, conjugate that element's two fixed points to 0,∞. If every nonidentity element has order two, choose one with fixed points 0,∞; the subgroup acts on this pair with image of size at most two and kernel contained in {z,−z}. A nonidentity Möbius transformation has one or two distinct fixed points on the Riemann sphere. If there is one, send it to infinity; the resulting affine map cannot have slope different from one, since that would give another fixed point. It is a nonzero translation, which a scaling conjugates to z+1. The identity is the scaling μ=1. Fixed-point sets are carried bijectively under conjugacy, so a translation is not conjugate to a scaling.

Comparing (e,v)(h,w) and (h,w)(e,v) shows that a translation is central precisely when its vector is fixed by the entire action. If H is itself abelian, the whole semidirect product is abelian exactly when the action is trivial. For H=(R,+), V=R2, and determinant-one linear actions fixing the first coordinate vector, ρ(x)=(10​r(x)1​), where r is an additive function. Without a regularity assumption, it need not be r(x)=cx.

Words: 88
Semidirect product OurBigBook.com
If N=⟨A∣R⟩ and H=⟨B∣S⟩ have finite group presentations and ϕ:H→Aut(N) is an action, choose a word wb,a​(A) representing ϕ(b)(a). Then N⋊ϕ​H has the finite presentation
⟨A,B∣R,S, bab−1=wb,a​(A) (a∈A,b∈B)⟩.
(67)
The action automorphisms also let these relations rewrite conjugation by inverse generators. Every word becomes an A-word followed by a B-word. The natural map to the semidirect product is injective because its triviality forces the B-word to be trivial using S and then the A-word to be trivial using R.

Words: 95
Semidirect product OurBigBook.com
If N is an elementary abelian normal subgroup and ∣G/N∣ is prime to its characteristic, the extension splits and its complements are conjugate by N. In additive notation an extension cocycle satisfies f(h,k)+f(hk,t)=hf(k,t)+f(h,kt). Averaging over t gives f(h,k)=b(h)+hb(k)−b(hk), where b(h)=∣G/N∣−1∑t​f(h,t). Changing the section by b removes the cocycle. For two complements the difference cocycle has d(hk)=d(h)+hd(k); averaging gives d(h)=b−hb, which is conjugation by an element of N. These arguments use invertibility of the group order on N and underlie Hall conjugacy in soluble groups.

Its identity is (0,0) and inverse is (−x,−a−xu); associativity follows by expanding both bracketings. Projection onto the first coordinate is a group homomorphism with normal cyclic kernel of order p. Under the change U=a−xu, multiplication becomes (x,U)(y,V)=(x+y,U+a−xV), the semidirect product of the additive prime field by the cyclic group of order p−1. The group is abelian precisely when a=1; a need not be a generator of the multiplicative field group.

Words: 1k Articles: 30
Group theory OurBigBook.com
A solvable group has a subnormal series whose factor groups are abelian.

Supersolvable group

Words: 64
Solvable group OurBigBook.com
A finite group is supersolvable if it has a normal series of a group whose nontrivial factors are cyclic of prime order. This is stronger than solubility, because the individual terms must be normal in the ambient group. For instance, A4​ is soluble via its normal Klein four-group, but is not supersolvable: it has no normal subgroup of order two or three with which such a series could begin.

Finitely generated soluble torsion groups are finite

Words: 65
Solvable group OurBigBook.com
A finitely generated abelian group whose elements all have finite order is finite. Induct on derived length for a finitely generated soluble group with this property. Its abelianization is finite, so its commutator subgroup has finite index and is finitely generated by Schreier's lemma. That subgroup is soluble of smaller derived length and is still a torsion group, hence finite by induction. The ambient group is a finite extension of it and is finite.

Virtually solvable group

Words: 139 Articles: 1
Solvable group OurBigBook.com
A group is virtually solvable, or virtually soluble, when it contains a solvable group as a finite-index subgroup. This is preserved under subgroups, quotients and group extensions. The extension proof can use a finite-index characteristic soluble subgroup of the kernel, followed by centralizing the resulting finite normal kernel. Finite generation is not required for these closure properties.

Finite-index characteristic soluble subgroup

Words: 91
Virtually solvable group OurBigBook.com
Every virtually soluble group K has a soluble characteristic subgroup of finite index. First take a soluble normal subgroup K0​ of finite index by the subgroup core construction. Choose a soluble normal subgroup R⊇K0​ maximizing its image size in the finite quotient K/K0​. For every soluble normal subgroup S, the product RS is soluble, because its quotient by R is a quotient of S. Maximality forces S≤R. Hence R is the unique largest soluble normal subgroup and is invariant under all automorphisms. This avoids incorrectly intersecting infinitely many conjugates when proving closure under group extensions.

A group is metabelian when its commutator subgroup is abelian, equivalently when its derived length is at most two.

Finite metabelian groups are monomial

Words: 74
Metabelian group OurBigBook.com
Let L◃G and both L,G/L be abelian. For an irreducible G-module, choose a subgroup A⊇L of maximal order whose restriction contains a linear character φ. Every subgroup containing L is normal. If an element x∈/A stabilizes φ, its action on the nonzero φ-isotypic component has an eigenvector; that line is invariant under ⟨A,x⟩ and affords a larger linear constituent, contradicting maximality. Thus IG​(φ)=A, and the Clifford correspondence gives χ=φG.

Polycyclic group

Words: 190 Articles: 3
Solvable group OurBigBook.com
A group is polycyclic when it has a subnormal series with cyclic factors. Every subgroup and quotient of a polycyclic group is finitely generated, and extensions of polycyclic groups are polycyclic.

Polycyclic groups are virtually poly-infinite cyclic

Words: 49
Polycyclic group OurBigBook.com
Every polycyclic group has a finite-index subgroup with a series whose nontrivial factors are infinite cyclic. This is the polycyclic finite-index lemma; it also supplies torsion-free finite-index subgroups. Such a subgroup is a poly-infinite cyclic group. Combining its series with the extension rule for Poincare duality groups makes it a duality group of dimension its Hirsch length.

Hirsch length (h(G))

Words: 42
Polycyclic group OurBigBook.com
The Hirsch length of a polycyclic group counts infinite cyclic factors in a polycyclic series. Refinement shows it is independent of the series, additive in extensions, and unchanged in finite-index subgroups. A finite-index poly-infinite cyclic group has one infinite cyclic factor for each unit of Hirsch length.

Poly-infinite cyclic group

Words: 68
Polycyclic group OurBigBook.com
A poly-infinite cyclic group has a finite subnormal series all of whose nontrivial factors are infinite cyclic groups. Intersecting its series with a subgroup again gives trivial or infinite cyclic factors; repetitions may be deleted. Splicing a kernel series with the preimage of a quotient series proves closure under extensions. Such groups are finitely presented groups: induct on the series, split the last extension by an infinite cyclic quotient, and use finite presentation of a semidirect product.

Nilpotent group OurBigBook.com
Every finitely generated torsion-free group which is a nilpotent group embeds as a discrete cocompact subgroup of a unique simply connected nilpotent real Lie group. Its dimension equals the group's integral cohomological dimension of a group. In dimension three the Lie algebra is either abelian or has a basis with a single nonzero bracket [Y,T]=X, giving the real Heisenberg group.

These factors are central, and γc−1​(G) centralizes G′, so replacing xi​ by xi​yi​ absorbs the error. A finite group is nilpotent exactly when it is the direct product of groups of its Sylow subgroups. Word collection in a two-step nilpotent group
Words: 66
Two-step nilpotent group OurBigBook.com
In a two-generated two-step nilpotent group, use c=[x,y]=x−1y−1xy. Centrality of c gives yx=xyc−1, so every word collects to xaybcr. The multiplication of these collected expressions is (a,b,r)(a′,b′,r′)=(a+a′,b+b′,r+r′−a′b). Relations on the central commutator can reduce r modulo its order. To turn collection into a word problem for a group algorithm, one must also prove the independence of the remaining coordinates, for example by constructing a group with that cocycle multiplication.

A finitely generated group has exponential growth when the number of elements represented by words of length at most n is bounded below by cn for some c>1 and all sufficiently large n. The property is independent of the chosen finite generating set.

The exponent of a finite group is the least common multiple of the orders of all its elements.
Every finite group is a torsion group; its exponent is a common multiple of the order of a group element for every element.

For any prime divisor q of the group order, Cauchy theorem for groups gives an element of order q, forcing q=p. This statement does not imply that the group is abelian; odd-characteristic upper unitriangular groups provide counterexamples.

Group theory OurBigBook.com
The order of an element is the least positive power equal to the identity and divides the order of a finite group.
This is the order of a group element in the finite setting, one use of order (group theory).

Order (group theory)

Words: 43
Group theory OurBigBook.com
In group theory, order can mean the cardinality of a group or the least positive n for which a group element g satisfies gn=e. If no such n exists, the element has infinite order. For a finite group, Lagrange's theorem implies that each element order divides the group order.
